This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
For any integer $n=\prod p^{k_p}$ let $Q_2(n)$ be the powerful part of $n$, so that\[Q_2(n) = \prod_{\substack{p\\ k_p\geq 2}}p^{k_p}.\]Is it true that, for every $\epsilon>0$ and $\ell\geq 1$, if $n$ is sufficiently large then\[Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))<n^{2+\epsilon}?\]If $\ell\geq 2$ then is\[\limsup_{n\to \infty}\frac{Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))}{n^2}\]infinite? 
If $\ell\geq 2$ then is\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))}{n^{\ell+1}}=0?\]
#935: [Er76d]
number theory | 
powerful
Erdős [Er76d] writes that if this is true then it 'seems very difficult to prove'. 
A result of Mahler implies, for every $\ell\geq 1$,\[\limsup_{n\to \infty}\frac{Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))}{n^2}\geq 1.\]All these questions can be asked replacing $Q_2$ by $Q_r$ for $r>2$, only keeping those prime powers with exponent $\geq r$.
The second part of this problem is essentially the same (up to constants) as [367]. The construction given there by van Doorn (also given by Aletheia [Fe26]) proves the second part in the affirmative, since a construction via solutions to the Pell equation $x^2-8y^2=1$ implies\[\limsup_{n\to \infty}\frac{Q_2(n(n+1)(n+2))}{n^2}=\infty.\]In [Fe26] it is similarly noted that the ABC conjecture implies a positive answer to the third question.
Additional thanks to: Superhuman Reasoning team at Google DeepMind and Wouter van Doorn

 This question is essentially the same as #367 (although I do note that we look at the powerful part of the product here, as opposed to the product of the powerful parts. But that changes at most a constant). In particular, the construction by Aletheia is also the one found in the comments on #367 (even though they only show unboundedness of the ratio, as opposed to the extra log-term we got here). It is certainly possible that Aletheia came up with it independently, but reading the Aletheia paper they do write that this was done early December 2025, roughly two weeks after the comments on #367.
(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

 Yes, that is probably the case. In fact, someone on our team pointed out that the solution candidate to Erdos-281 was arguably close to correct. Given the pace of improvements to the base model and agent, though, it would be more efficient for a team of our size to keep rerunning the open problems rather than examining old outputs. Personally I would only be inclined to revisit the Erdos problems after improving the model's capability substantially. To find more problems that can be solved with the current capability, I think it would be better to just give our tools to the public. 
The Erdos problems were actually not a consideration when building Aletheia; we ran them later when it became clear that they would become a common discussion point. It turned out to be useful for us to get a large-scale picture of the model's capabilities, but I think our team is happy to leave the results as a case study instead of trying to optimize the number of Erdos problems solved. We each have our own pet research problems that we want to get back to :)
P.S. Tonight's arXiv update will move our Erdos-935 result to the "Independent Rediscovery" section, crediting Woett appropriately.
